title: PAUL SAID, “DO NOT DEPRIVE EACH OTHER”—BUT READ THE WORDS THAT COME NEXT
paragraphs:
PAUL SAID, “DO NOT DEPRIVE EACH OTHER”—BUT READ THE WORDS THAT COME NEXT
One of the Bible’s most intimate teachings about marriage has sometimes been reduced to a demand. But when you read what Paul actually wrote, you discover something far more beautiful: mutuality, tenderness, spiritual responsibility—and a marriage in which neither spouse is given permission to treat the other like property.
There are Bible verses people remember because they comfort us.
And then there are Bible verses people remember because someone once used them against us.
For some married Christians, 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 belongs painfully close to the second category.
Maybe you have heard it quoted during an argument.
“Your body belongs to me.”
Maybe you heard, “The Bible says you cannot deprive your spouse.”
Maybe Scripture was brought into a bedroom already filled with resentment, rejection, exhaustion, unresolved wounds, loneliness, or tears.
And suddenly a passage intended to teach Christian husbands and wives about mutual devotion sounded less like love...
and more like leverage.
But there is something in Paul's actual words that we cannot afford to miss.
Something extraordinarily important.
Read carefully.
Paul did tell married believers not to deprive one another.
But he did not stop there.
He wrote:
“Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους, εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν...”
“Mē apostereite allēlous, ei mēti an ek symphōnou pros kairon...”
The heart of the sentence is unmistakably mutual.
“Do not deprive one another, except by mutual agreement for a time...”
—1 Corinthians 7:5
That little Greek expression deserves to slow us down:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual consent.
Together.
The word is related to the idea from which we get “symphony”—different voices sounding together in agreement.
And that changes the atmosphere of the passage.
Because Paul is not describing one spouse exercising unrestricted power over another.
He is describing two people belonging to one another in covenant love.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Paul begins:
“Τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω...”
Let the husband render to his wife what is due to her.
Then immediately:
“ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί.”
And likewise the wife to her husband.
That word matters.
Likewise.
Not husband only.
Not wife only.
Both.
Then Paul says something that would have landed with tremendous force in the ancient world:
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ...”
The wife does not exercise authority over her body independently of her husband.
But before anyone turns that sentence into a weapon, Paul immediately turns the language around:
“ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.”
Likewise, the husband does not exercise authority over his own body independently of his wife.
Read that again.
The husband too.
Paul does not hand the husband ownership and leave the wife powerless.
He places husband and wife under a startlingly reciprocal obligation.
Her body matters to him.
His body matters to her.
Her needs matter.
His needs matter.
Her vulnerability matters.
His vulnerability matters.
Marriage is not supposed to become two people asking, “What can I demand from you?”
Christian marriage moves toward a far more Christlike question:
“How can I faithfully give myself to you in love?”
That is completely different.
And this is where some marriages desperately need healing.
Because intimacy can quietly become a battlefield.
One spouse feels rejected.
The other feels pressured.
One stops initiating because rejection hurts too much.
The other begins dreading affection because every hug seems to carry an expectation.
Days become weeks.
Tenderness becomes tension.
Nobody says what is actually happening.
Then resentment starts translating everything.
“I’m tired” becomes “I don't want you.”
“Not tonight” becomes “You're unattractive.”
“Why don't you ever initiate?” becomes “You only care about my body.”
Two wounded people sleep inches apart...
while feeling miles away.
And somewhere inside that silence, both may wonder:
How did we get here?
Paul refuses to treat sexual intimacy as insignificant.
But neither does his language give Christians permission to turn intimacy into domination.
The command itself is reciprocal: “Do not deprive one another.”
And when abstinence is chosen for concentrated prayer, Paul describes it as temporary and mutually agreed upon.
Not punishment.
Not manipulation.
Not revenge.
Not spiritual blackmail.
Not, “You made me angry, so I will make you suffer.”
Not, “If you really loved God, you would do what I want.”
Not, “The Bible says your body belongs to me, so you have no voice.”
That last statement takes half of Paul's sentence and amputates the other half.
Because Paul says the husband belongs to the wife in the same reciprocal sense.
This is covenant language, not a license for coercion.
Christian marriage is never made holier by using Scripture to frighten a spouse into submission to selfish desire.
The same New Testament that speaks about marital obligation commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Think about that standard.
Christ does not exploit His Bride.
Christ gives Himself for His Bride.
Christ does not crush the vulnerable.
Christ moves toward them with sacrificial love.
So whenever we interpret marital intimacy in a supposedly “biblical” way that produces selfish domination while conveniently removing Christlike love, we have missed something fundamental.
Jesus changes the question.
Not merely:
“What am I owed?”
But:
“How can I love?”
That question can expose both spouses.
Because selfishness does not wear only one face.
There can be selfish demanding.
And there can also be selfish withholding.
There can be coercion.
There can also be manipulation through rejection.
There can be pressure.
There can be punishment.
There can be entitlement.
There can be indifference.
And sometimes there is something else entirely.
Pain.
Trauma.
Illness.
Hormonal changes.
Pregnancy.
Childbirth recovery.
Medication.
Exhaustion.
Depression.
Grief.
Past sexual wounds.
Fear.
Relational betrayal.
A marriage carrying years of unresolved hurt.
Those realities should not be bulldozed with a Bible verse.
They should invite compassion, honesty, patience, wise pastoral care when appropriate, and sometimes professional medical or counseling help.
Because your spouse is not a theological problem to solve.
Your spouse is a human being to love.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been silently hurting because intimacy disappeared from your marriage a long time ago.
You love Jesus.
You love your spouse.
But something broke.
Maybe nobody cheated.
Nobody packed a suitcase.
Nobody filed papers.
You still sit together at church.
You still smile in family photographs.
People probably think everything is fine.
But when the lights go out...
there is a silence nobody else hears.
Please hear this carefully.
The answer is not pretending the problem doesn't matter.
And the answer is not forcing intimacy either.
The Gospel gives us another road.
Truth.
Grace.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Patience.
Honest conversation.
Sacrificial love.
Restoration.
Sometimes the most intimate sentence a husband or wife can speak is not whispered beneath the sheets.
Sometimes it is spoken across a kitchen table with trembling hands:
“Tell me where I hurt you.”
And then...
listen.
Not to defend yourself.
Not to collect ammunition.
Not to prepare your rebuttal.
Listen because covenant love wants truth more than victory.
Maybe you discover that your spouse has felt unwanted for years.
Maybe you discover that your spouse has felt pressured for years.
Maybe both are true.
Maybe the person beside you has been carrying something you never understood because you were interpreting everything through your own pain.
This is where Jesus enters places pride cannot heal.
Because Christ does not merely teach us how to win marital arguments.
He teaches sinners how to die to themselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not demand that guilty people make themselves worthy before He loved them.
He gave Himself.
“For while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
That is the gravitational center of Christian marriage.
Not sex.
Not romance.
Not compatibility.
Not even happiness.
Christ.
A crucified and risen Savior teaching two imperfect people what covenant faithfulness looks like.
That does not mean tolerating abuse.
It does not mean remaining silent about coercion.
It does not mean pretending serious sin is harmless.
Grace never requires calling darkness light.
But grace does mean that broken people do not have to remain exactly where their brokenness left them.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still exposes selfishness without abandoning the sinner.
Jesus still teaches husbands how to become tender.
Jesus still teaches wives how to become tender.
Jesus still heals what shame told you could never be spoken about.
And maybe that is why this passage needs to be recovered.
Because Paul's vision is bigger than “give your spouse sex.”
His words confront a culture of self-ownership with covenant mutuality.
The husband gives himself.
The wife gives herself.
Neither gets to make marriage entirely about “me.”
Even temporary abstinence for spiritual devotion is something Paul envisions as agreed upon together and limited in duration.
Together.
There is that word again.
Maybe your marriage does not need another argument about who is right.
Maybe it needs two people kneeling before Jesus saying:
“Lord, show me where I became selfish.”
“Show me where resentment hardened me.”
“Show me where I stopped listening.”
“Show me where I used affection as leverage.”
“Show me where I demanded instead of loved.”
“Show me where I withheld instead of communicating.”
“Show me what my spouse has been trying to tell me.”
“Teach me to love like You.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because Jesus may answer it.
He may expose something you have spent years explaining away.
But exposure in the hands of Christ is not the end of the story.
Peter was exposed.
Thomas was exposed.
The woman at the well was exposed.
Paul himself was exposed.
The cross exposes us all.
And then grace begins rewriting what sin tried to finish.
That is the Gospel.
Not “clean yourself up so Jesus might accept you.”
But Christ meeting sinners in truth, calling us to repentance, forgiving those who come to Him, and transforming us by grace.
So husband...
your wife is not an object God gave you to satisfy yourself.
She is someone you have been called to love sacrificially.
And wife...
your husband is not an emotional machine who should simply endure rejection without being affected.
He is someone you have been called to love faithfully.
Both of you belong first to Jesus.
Both of you need grace.
Both of you need repentance.
Both of you need tenderness.
Both of you need truth.
And both of you should be able to speak honestly without fearing that Scripture will be turned into a weapon against you.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable.
Don't run from that discomfort too quickly.
Take it to Jesus.
If you have used Scripture selfishly, repent.
If you have deliberately used intimacy or its absence to punish your spouse, repent.
If resentment has become your secret companion, bring it into the light.
If your spouse has wounded you, seek truth and healing rather than pretending nothing happened.
If your marriage is healthy, guard it with humility.
And if your marriage is struggling badly, asking for wise help is not an admission that Jesus failed.
Sometimes seeking help is one of the ways we stop hiding and begin walking in truth.
Or, if the battle is deeply personal:
“Pray for me.”
You do not owe strangers the details.
But sometimes bringing even three honest words into the light is the beginning of refusing to hide.
Your testimony may become another couple's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because every marriage problem can be solved by rereading a Facebook post, but because there may come a night when hurt becomes louder than wisdom and you need to remember:
Biblical intimacy is covenantal, reciprocal, truthful, tender, and centered on Christ.
Send it privately to the couple who may be struggling silently.
And please never use this article as ammunition against your spouse.
Use it as a mirror before God.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can itself become an act offered to God's glory when it is done freely, faithfully, and from a heart that wants biblical truth to reach more people. Sharing these articles matters too.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
go back to the Word.
Go back to Christ.
Go back to your spouse with humility instead of ammunition.
Because maybe the most important thing Paul said in this passage was hidden in plain sight all along.
Not husband against wife.
Not wife against husband.
Not “your body exists for me.”
One another.
And somewhere tonight, behind a closed bedroom door, two wounded people may finally stop asking, “What do you owe me?”
...and begin asking,
“Jesus, teach me how to love the person You entrusted to me.”
That may be where the scandal ends.
And grace begins rewriting everything.
The marriage you thought was dying may not need another weaponized Bible verse—it may need two surrendered hearts meeting Jesus at the same cross.
